q: Motion along a straight line is called linear motion.
e: This is the exact definition of linear motion provided in the text.

q: In a linear motion, the magnitude of the displacement is equal to the distance moved.
e: Because the path is straight, the path length equals the magnitude of the displacement vector.

q: In a linear motion, the magnitude of the velocity is also equal to the speed.
e: For straight-line motion without direction changes, speed and velocity magnitude are identical.

q: The most simplest type of motion is the linear motion with constant velocity.
e: This is stated explicitly in the text as the simplest type of motion.

q: Since the velocity is constant, the acceleration is non-zero.
e: Since the velocity is constant, there is no change in velocity, so the acceleration is zero.

q: As the body is moving with a non-varying velocity, the instantaneous velocity and average velocity are the same.
e: Constant velocity means the velocity at any instant equals the average over any interval.

q: In describing the equations of motion we shall use the vector notation.
e: The text states we shall not use vector notation, but rather positive and negative signs for direction.

q: We will use positive (+) and negative (-) signs to describe the two opposite directions along a straight line.
e: This is the stated convention for handling direction in 1D equations of motion.

q: The equation of motion for a linear motion with constant velocity is $v = \frac{s}{t}$.
e: This is the fundamental equation for constant velocity motion.

q: If the rate of change of velocity is constant, the acceleration is said to be constant.
e: A constant rate of change of velocity is the definition of constant acceleration.

q: If a body is moving with a constant acceleration of $5 \text{ m s}^{-2}$, the velocity of the body changes by $5 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ in every second.
e: This is the exact example provided in the text to illustrate constant acceleration.

q: Since the acceleration is constant, the instantaneous acceleration and average acceleration are different.
e: Since the acceleration is constant, the instantaneous acceleration and average acceleration are the same.

q: The equation $v = v_0 + at$ is an equation of motion for constant acceleration.
e: This is Eq. (2.6), a fundamental equation of motion for constant acceleration.

q: The equation $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2as$ is an equation of motion for constant acceleration.
e: This is Eq. (2.7), relating velocity, acceleration, and displacement without time.

q: The equation $s = v_0 t + \frac{1}{2}at^2$ is derived from other equations of motion.
e: The text explicitly states this equation is derived from Eqs. (2.6), (2.9), and (2.10).

q: The equation $s = \bar{v}t$ is an equation of motion where $\bar{v}$ is average velocity.
e: This is Eq. (2.9), correctly identifying $\bar{v}$ as average velocity.

q: The equation $\bar{v} = \frac{v_0 + v}{2}$ is valid for motion with constant acceleration.
e: This is Eq. (2.10), which gives the average velocity for constant acceleration.

q: Except Eq. (2.7), the rest equations can be expressed in vector form.
e: The text explicitly notes that Eq. (2.7) cannot be expressed in vector form, while the others can.

q: The SI unit of displacement is centimetre (cm).
e: The SI (MKS) unit of displacement is the metre (m), while centimetre is the CGS unit.

q: The CGS unit of velocity is $\text{cm s}^{-1}$.
e: This matches the CGS column in Table 2.1 of the text.

q: The FPS unit of acceleration is $\text{ft s}^{-2}$.
e: This matches the FPS column in Table 2.1 of the text.

q: The unit $\text{m s}^{-2}$ means metre per second square.
e: This is the exact verbal description of the SI unit of acceleration provided in the text.
